prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength enable timekeeping with uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks with Katori and Ye as my preferred and final position, and I did not change the configuration after round 1; what changed is how I would word the claim. The new principle, which the chair and Mehlig and Pearce asked us to name, is specific: the trap light shift is made to cancel for the clock transition at a magic wavelength, so that many neutral atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime at once. That removes Doppler and recoil broadening while keeping the statistical power of an ensemble, and neither the 2005 comb prize nor the 2012 prize on controlling single trapped ions delivered that combination. The test of whether it is an invention rather than a refinement is what happened next: independent groups in several countries reproduced it in Sr, Yb and Hg and compared clocks at about 1e-18, which an incremental tweak would not have achieved. I take the citation to rest on both the concept and the demonstrated performance, because the concept without the control of blackbody, higher-order light-shift and hyperpolarisability effects would not have produced a clock, and the performance without the concept would not exist. I also want the text to stand on what has been shown and not on the redefinition of the second, as Kroll argued.
statement.case_against: The honest weak points are unchanged. Takamoto and Ido made the first Sr lattice-clock demonstration, and Lemonde, Ludlow and others contributed to the cross-checks and the systematic evaluation; a two-name prize leaves all of them out, and I cannot resolve their relative priority from the material in front of us. Ye's reputation rests partly on comb and ultrastable-laser work that earlier prizes touched, so the citation must credit him for the lattice clock only. A reasonable colleague can still read the lineage as already honoured twice. Finally, I flagged in round 1 that agreement among members with an atomic-physics vantage is weak evidence, and I still hold that; I take some comfort that members outside AMO have said the conceptual step is real, but it remains a judgement of kind and not a measurement.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that founding proposers and leaders are an acceptable proxy for the ATLAS and CMS discovery, that the 2013 prize covered only theory, and that a precision-metrology advance does not answer a question comparable to the origin of mass; he nonetheless says he would not object strongly if the committee settled on Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I accept the second and third points: the 2013 prize does not cover the observation, and as a statement about the Standard Model the Higgs result is more consequential than any clock. I still cannot support B026, because the chair asked for a principle and none has been given. Founding leadership says who conceived and built the instruments, not who made the 2012 observation, and if one chose spokespersons or analysis leaders instead the three names would be different people. I would reconsider only if someone states what each of Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee did for the observation itself. His willingness to accept B042 is useful evidence for me, since he has no atomic-physics stake and judges by discovery of nature.

responses.point: Pearce prefers IceCube as a new observational channel and regards the clocks as a refinement of capabilities that the 2005 and 2012 prizes largely created, while saying he would be comfortable with B042 as the prize and listing it as his first alternative.
responses.response: I think the distinction between a new observational channel and a refinement is fair as a description of character, but I do not accept it as a ranking. A clock at 1e-18 observes things no earlier clock could, such as the gravitational redshift over a millimetre scale, and it supplies new tests of constants and dark matter, so it also opens a channel, if a quieter one. On IceCube, I agree the diffuse flux is secure, but source identification rests on one association and the Baikal, DUMAND and AMANDA credit is not settled in a two-name prize. I also think it right that the committee decides whether his Fermi-LAT link calls for recusal on B029; it is collaboration-level and I would not insist on it, but it argues for settling B029 by evidence rather than by his advocacy. Since he already lists B042 as his fallback, I read our positions as closer than the first-place counts suggest.

responses.point: Mehlig asks what new principle the lattice clock adds beyond a superb implementation, says that magic-wavelength, many-atom Lamb-Dicke interrogation would be a fair claim, and says he would be comfortable with B042 as a compromise if B034 cannot gather support; he also argues for waiting on twisted bilayer graphene.
responses.response: That is the answer I would give, and I am glad it satisfies a statistical physicist who does not work near the field. On his own choice, I find the KPZ-to-random-matrix link and the liquid-crystal experiment elegant, and I cannot assess the exact-solution literature well. But he states the weaknesses himself: Parisi is outside the trio, the exact-solution contributors are outside it, and experimental universality rests on a narrow base. On those grounds I cannot see B034 as ready as a three-person prize. I agree with his caution on B054, where Cao's omission and the unresolved pairing mechanism argue for waiting.

responses.point: Johansson now prefers B042 with the same names and the concept-and-performance citation, would keep thorium out of the discussion, and says Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde contributed to the first measurements and cross-checks, which a two-person prize leaves out.
responses.response: I agree with his wording and with keeping the nuclear clock out; it is a separate, still developing result, and the citation should name only the lattice architecture and its performance. His honesty about leaving Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde out is the point that matters most to me. I would not hide it: the committee should record that the concept and its realisation are credited to Katori and Ye and that the others belong to the broader development. I also respect his decision to step back from circuit QED on grounds of his own connection, and I would still count B033 and B053 together as the main quantum-technology alternatives for a later year.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers TMR, now treats B042 as his first alternative and a serious rival after reading the arguments, and says the Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde problem is the same kind of credit problem he accepts in his own case.
responses.response: I take that as the most substantive movement from outside AMO. I would ask him to compare the credit gaps directly: for B042 the omitted names come at the edges of a concept and a record that Katori and Ye identifiably delivered, whereas for B037 his own account says the coherent-MgO step, the one that made the effect large, involves Yuasa and Djayaprawira. I do not claim that settles it, because TMR physics is outside my own field and I cannot judge the 2007 overlap. If he were willing to support B042 in the vote I would regard that as a stronger endorsement than a count of AMO members.

uncertainties: Whether Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde have a priority claim on the first Sr lattice-clock demonstration that the credit to Katori and Ye does not adequately cover; I cannot verify the dates from the committee material.

How strongly members outside AMO believe the magic-wavelength, many-atom architecture is a distinct principle rather than a refinement of clock work already honoured in 2005 and 2012; Danielsson, Eriksson, Mehlig and Pearce have been supportive but only conditionally.
Whether the Higgs configuration can ever be given a principled three-name credit; if a member supplies one, B026 may outrank B042 on scientific weight.
Whether the committee will want to wait for the redefinition of the second or for the thorium work before honouring clocks; I do not think it should, but I may be wrong about how others read timing.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has appeared for B042: my profile documents no collaboration, supervision or institutional tie to Hidetoshi Katori or Jun Ye, and nothing in round 1 changes that. I remain a theoretical atomic physicist, so I am close to the field in expertise and I have said so in the arguments above. I again disclose documented collaborations with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and with Reinhold Schuch, Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti and Paul Indelicato; none concerns a credited name on this shortlist, but I would raise it if an attosecond ballot came up. I note the chair's disclosed Fermi-LAT link to B029 and Johansson's disclosed link to B033, and I leave their recusal to the committee.
